Managers must explain the portfolio constraints and investment guidelines that maintain that liquidity bias, and demonstrate that they can handle frequent monthly flows of about $10–25 million, occasionally $50–100 million. NMSIC then tests *realizability and cost*: for an assumed $500 million account, bidders estimate the days to sell 10%, 25%, 50%, 75% and 100% with minimal market impact; full-liquidation costs over 3, 7, 15 and 30 days; and the share of holdings needing more than 30 days. ## Outsourced-provider oversight checklist

Use this at appointment, at least annually thereafter, and after a material change or incident. For each item, record **owner, evidence reviewed, finding, remediation deadline, and next review date**. The DDQs supply diligence questions; the review cadence and evidence requests below are a proposed way to turn them into oversight controls.

### 1. Provider inventory and accountability
- [ ] List every outsourced control provider and forestry manager or third-party operator, its services, operating locations, subcontractors, and the person accountable for oversight.
- [ ] Confirm each provider’s legal identity, applicable regulatory status, ownership, and relevant qualifications. Identify changes in ownership, personnel, scope, or location that require reassessment.
- [ ] Document a pre-appointment risk assessment and a risk-based monitoring plan. For sub-distributors, confirm applicable distribution and AML regulatory status, domicile, and operating countries.
- [ ] Put obligations in writing: scope, compliance requirements, periodic reporting, monitoring and access to evidence, incident escalation, remediation, and liability for material breach where appropriate.

*Evidence:* provider register, regulatory checks, risk assessment, signed agreement, reporting schedule. The distributor DDQ expressly asks about initial diligence, contracts, ongoing monitoring, and sub-distributor locations; it also asks whether outsourced internal audit, risk, compliance, or AML/CTF functions receive oversight and due diligence. (Investment Funds Distributor DDQ, pp. 9, 11.)

### 2. Operational control functions
- [ ] **Risk and compliance:** Identify who performs each function, how independence and management reporting work, and how compliance with internal policies is monitored. Obtain independent-testing results, material findings, overdue actions, and evidence of closure.
- [ ] **Internal audit:** Confirm audit coverage of relevant activities and AML/CTF, the date of the last review, findings, and whether unresolved issues have been escalated.
- [ ] **AML/CTF and financial crime:** Check responsibility for underlying-client KYC/CDD, beneficial-owner identification, risk-based reviews, sanctions and PEP screening, transaction monitoring, suspicious-activity reporting, staff training, and legally required record retention. Where sub-distributors perform these tasks, obtain their AML/KYC certification or equivalent-jurisdiction rationale.
- [ ] **Information and resilience:** Review tested client-data safeguards, IT security and confidentiality, data retention/deletion, and business-continuity and disaster-recovery plans. Record tests, failures, and corrective actions.
- [ ] **Conduct and distribution, where relevant:** Check product approval, investor eligibility and suitability, jurisdiction and marketing restrictions, required investor documents, remuneration and inducement controls, complaint escalation, and oversight of sub-distributors. Review sanctions, regulatory actions, and material audit findings rather than relying on a yes/no attestation.

*Evidence:* policies, control-testing reports, audit reports, training records, exception logs, sample monitoring reports, continuity-test results, complaint and regulatory-action registers. (Investment Funds Distributor DDQ, pp. 6–15.)

### 3. Forestry-operator ESG capability and incidents
- [ ] **Capability:** Identify who oversees and who implements ESG integration at the manager and operator; assess their qualifications, staffing, training, and external expertise. Record capability gaps and the actions to close them.
- [ ] **Standards and asset controls:** Review the forestry ESG policy and applicable commitments. Verify the scope, dates, certificates, and available audit findings for FSC/PEFC certification—or the explanation and alignment plan where certification is unavailable. Check processes for legal title and customary land-tenure rights.
- [ ] **Asset monitoring:** Agree what ESG performance data operators collect, how often it is checked, who verifies it, and whether targets are set. Review stewardship actions and assessment of climate-risk exposure and resilience.
- [ ] **Material incidents:** Require the operator to identify, promptly escalate, investigate, and address material ESG incidents. For each incident, record affected assets, impacts, immediate response, root cause, corrective action, owner, completion evidence, and recurrence monitoring. Confirm how and when the manager informs investors; do not treat a closed incident as resolved without checking the remedy.
- [ ] **Investor reporting:** Obtain sample ESG disclosures, confirm reporting channels and frequency, put ESG on investor-meeting agendas, and check that material-incident disclosures are consistent with the underlying incident record.

*Evidence:* ESG policy, role and training records, certification and audit documents, asset-level data and targets, climate assessment, incident log, corrective-action evidence, investor reports. PRI’s forestry DDQ specifically asks how managers assess third-party operators’ ESG expertise, monitor asset performance, ensure responses to material incidents, and disclose those incidents to investors. (Responsible Investment DDQ for Forestry Investors, p. 2, questions 1.1–1.4, 2.1–2.2, 3.3, 4.1–4.3, 4.7, 5.1–5.4.)

**Decision gate:** Approve or continue a provider only with documented acceptance of residual risks. Escalate material incidents, regulatory or audit findings, repeated data gaps, and overdue remediation to the accountable oversight body; reassess the mandate if corrective action is ineffective.

1. **Operative policy and implementation status.** The full responsible-investment policy, its effective date and fund applicability; what is already implemented versus planned; and any formal ESG commitments in the LPA or side letters. Identify any standards, initiatives or reporting frameworks the GP claims to follow and the scope of each commitment. 2. **Climate governance documents.** The climate policy or equivalent mechanism that will apply by the fund’s first investment. If climate provisions sit in several documents, provide a map to them. The documents should show the fund’s climate stance and concrete action plans for both investment decisions and ownership—not just a statement of intent. [2025 Climate Module, Q1, p. 3](dwtyzx6upklss.cloudfront.net__private_equity_ddq_climatemodule_2025_70909__ba69e831.pdf#page=3)

3. **Named accountability and capability.** An organisation chart or responsibility matrix naming who oversees and who implements ESG and climate work, their qualifications and any external support. For climate, provide evidence of senior-level accountability—such as investment-committee or board terms of reference, role descriptions or remuneration provisions—and explain how oversight reaches strategy, major decisions and risk frameworks. Include staff training and access to specialist advice. [PRI LP DDQ, §§2.6–2.7, p. 2](d8g8t13e9vf2o.cloudfront.net__prilpresponsibleinvestmentddq_76200__5db863c3.pdf#page=2); [Climate Module, Q2, p. 4](dwtyzx6upklss.cloudfront.net__private_equity_ddq_climatemodule_2025_70909__ba69e831.pdf#page=4)

4. **Proof that governance operates in deals.** The materiality criteria and diligence procedures, plus redacted examples showing how ESG and material physical or transition climate findings reached the investment committee, affected approval or valuation, and entered deal documents or post-investment plans. The climate module asks which assessment tools and forward-looking data are used where relevant. [PRI LP DDQ, §§2.1–2.5, p. 2](d8g8t13e9vf2o.cloudfront.net__prilpresponsibleinvestmentddq_76200__5db863c3.pdf#page=2); [Climate Module, Q4, p. 6](dwtyzx6upklss.cloudfront.net__private_equity_ddq_climatemodule_2025_70909__ba69e831.pdf#page=6)

An ESG policy cover sheet establishes neither **what applies to this fund** nor **who implements it**. Ask the GP for the following evidence, using the PRI questionnaires as a diligence discussion rather than a pass/fail checklist:

1. **The operative policies and their status.** Obtain the full responsible-investment policy and any climate policy or other governance documents, with links to provisions spread across documents. Ask which provisions apply to this fund, when they take effect, what is already implemented versus planned, and the investment- and ownership-phase action plans. Identify the scope of any standards, initiatives or reporting commitments, and any ESG commitments in the LPA, fund documents or side letters. *[LP DDQ, questions 1.1–1.4, p. 2; Climate Module, questions 1–1.1, p. 3].*

2. **Named accountability and capability.** Request the senior body or roles accountable for this fund’s climate risks and opportunities, plus the people responsible for day-to-day ESG implementation, their qualifications and external support. Ask for terms of reference or role descriptions showing assigned duties; explain how ESG and climate enter strategy, major decisions and risk oversight, and what staff training or advice supports those duties. *[LP DDQ, questions 2.6–2.7, p. 2; Climate Module, questions 2–2.1, p. 4].*

3. **Proof the policy changes decisions.** Ask for the materiality criteria and process for identifying ESG and physical/transition climate risks and opportunities; examples from a recent fund; and redacted diligence, Investment Committee, deal-documentation or post-investment action-plan examples showing how findings affected approval, valuation or ownership plans. *[LP DDQ, questions 2.1–2.5, p. 2; Climate Module, questions 4–4.2, p. 6].*

4. **Ownership-phase oversight.** Request the portfolio-monitoring and board-engagement process, how company management’s ESG competence and resources are assessed, and examples of climate engagement, resilience or decarbonisation planning. If the GP says it will monitor climate KPIs or set fund decarbonisation goals, ask which metrics or goals, their time horizons, data methods, review cadence and any third-party validation. The module **asks whether** goals will be set; it does not require the GP to claim it has them. *[LP DDQ, questions 3.1–3.5, p. 2; Climate Module, questions 3–3.1 and 5–6.2, pp. 5, 7–8].*

5. **LP visibility and escalation.** Ask for sample ESG disclosures, whether ESG is discussed at LPAC or annual meetings, and the procedure for reporting and following up material ESG incidents. For climate, request the proposed LP reporting frameworks, targets and metrics, format, frequency and a recent-fund example if available. *[LP DDQ, questions 4.1–4.3, p. 2; Climate Module, questions 7–7.1, p. 9].*

The key follow-up is: **“Show us the fund-specific documents, accountable owners, operating procedures and examples that connect the cover sheet to actual decisions and oversight.”**
